video.title: The Most Profitable Business Everyone Overlooks

summary: Mike describes building a drone business that combines deer recovery, a pilot directory, drone sales and agricultural spraying. He says his agricultural spraying jobs can produce high profits, and explains that customers often need to see a live demonstration before hiring an operator. The conversation also covers pricing, equipment, licensing, marketing, and the growth of his business. Chris Koerner highlights the opportunity in agricultural spraying while noting the operational demands and regulatory steps.

speakers.name: Mike
speakers.description: Drone business operator; surname not stated.

ideas.name: Agricultural spray drone application service
ideas.one_liner: Use heavy-lift drones to apply farmer-supplied crop treatments, charging by acre.
ideas.business_model: Per-acre application service, sometimes with repeat applications during a crop season.
ideas.customer: Farmers who need crops or pasture sprayed and may not want to buy, operate, or maintain their own spray equipment.
ideas.problem: Farmers need crop treatments applied, including where wet ground, trees, power lines, or rough terrain limit other equipment.
ideas.offer: Bring a spray drone and trailer to the farm, mix the farmer's chosen product, and apply it to specified acres. The farmer supplies the chemical.

pricing.model: Per acre, with price varying by terrain, alternatives, and application volume.

price_points.label: Approximate price matching an airplane on suitable fields
Possible extra charge for five-gallon rather than two-gallon application

pricing.notes: Mike says operating cost is $3 to $3.74 per acre for the work he describes. The chemical is supplied separately by the farmer. Prices and costs are US claims.

acquisition_channels.details: Visit farms with the equipment and ask to demonstrate spraying with water over the farmer's crops. The guest says to get permission before flying over the land.

quote.text: The way that I would tell people to get a customer is you you have to go to the customer or get the customer come to you to do a demonstration.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Visit agricultural co-ops where farmers buy seed and chemicals, show the drone and trailer, and introduce the service.

quote.text: I went to co-ops like where the farmers buy their seed and chemical from. So I showed up there with my drones and my trailer doing exactly what you said.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: A demonstration can lead farmers and their friends to ask for the service or book it for a later season.

quote.text: We are flying at a farmer's field and there's an airplane next to us like ripping over his corn and he walks over and he's like, That's cool. You're spraying my corn next year.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Chris suggested scraping farmland ownership data and visiting owners. Mike objected to flying over a property without permission; the suggested outreach method was not established as something Mike did.

ideas.delivery: The operator travels to the farm with heavy-lift drones and a trailer, mixes the farmer's selected chemical, fills the drone, and sprays the crop. The drone can follow automated missions, but a person must be present to supervise, refill tanks, swap batteries, and manage equipment. Mike says he avoids recommending chemicals.
unit_economics_claims: Mike claimed operating costs of $3 to $3.74 per acre and prices commonly between $10 and $20 per acre.
Mike claimed he made $132,000 in 24 days and 'profited' $65,000 on a separate 8-day job, of which he says about $50,000 went to the bank (implying the $65k may be gross).
Mike said a 70% net margin was typical for the work he described; he said difficult rolling acres could produce 85% to 90% profit margins.
Mike said an example drone carries 26 gallons and can cover about 12 or 13 acres per load at two gallons per acre.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The operator needs spray equipment and a trailer; equipment purchase prices are not given.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated for an independent operator. The guest says one required FAA process can take three to four months; his separate Fastpass program may allow flying under his licensing in about ten days.

acquisition.how: Mike describes in-person farm visits and live demonstrations as the way to win customers. Software can help identify prospects, but it cannot perform the demonstration or close the relationship by itself.

onboarding.how: License checks, paperwork, understanding the farmer's fields and chosen product, and agreeing on application details require human coordination.

delivery.how: Automated flight missions handle much of the drone's route, but physical setup, chemical mixing, refilling, battery swaps, safety checks, and supervision require a person on site.

billing.how: Per-acre billing could be calculated from mapped acres and recorded work, but no automated billing system is described and a human would need to confirm completed work.

support.how: Farmers may need operational coordination, field-specific decisions, and a responsive operator; no automated support process is described.

uk_applicability.notes: Crop spraying and agricultural contractors exist in the UK, but the transcript's FAA certificates, US crop data, pricing, and operating assumptions do not transfer directly. UK aviation and pesticide rules would need to be followed.

risks: The service involves aircraft, pesticides, and heavy equipment, so licensing and compliance are central.
The guest says FAA authorization for heavy-lift spraying is difficult and that government processing can be slow.
Farmers may need to see the application work before buying; relying only on online discovery may not bring enough customers.
Season length, weather, crop type, field conditions, battery rotation, and repeat applications affect workload and revenue.
Mike advises not to recommend a farmer's chemical because a poor crop outcome could be blamed on both the product and the drone service.
The transcript's very high profit claims are the guest's own claims and are not independently verified.

ideas.name: Drone deer recovery service
ideas.one_liner: Use a thermal drone to locate deer that hunters shot but could not recover.
ideas.business_model: Per-recovery service fee, with a different stated fee depending on whether the deer is found.
ideas.customer: Hunters who have shot a deer and cannot locate it.
ideas.problem: Hunters may lose a wounded deer and want help finding it without walking through an area and disturbing other deer.
ideas.offer: Search the property with a thermal drone, identify a heat signature, and help the hunter recover the deer.

pricing.model: Per search, with a success-based price difference.

price_points.label: If the deer is not found

pricing.notes: Mike initially considered $250 to $350, then raised his stated prices after hearing feedback at an expo. He compared the service to a tracking dog that cost about $350.

acquisition_channels.details: Show thermal footage at the Northeast Ohio Sportsman Show using a simple booth, screen, sign, business cards, and magnets.

quote.text: I took that video to an outdoor show, a local outdoor show, and I just had a table with a cloth over it and an old iMac that I had.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Put flyers in local bow shops and rifle ranges; the flyers showed the drone, thermal view, and zoomed image.

quote.text: I printed off these brochures, like a a flyer, and I went to the local bow shops, uh local rifle ranges, that type of thing.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Hunters talked about the service with other hunters after seeing the demonstration or using it.

quote.text: And so once you got some people talking about it, they were just talking to their next people that they knew because yeah, word of mouth.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Mike started a YouTube channel alongside the service and used drone recovery content to publicize the category.

quote.text: when I came up with this business idea, it was part of the the whole thing. It was like, okay, this is my idea. I'm going to do it as a service, but I also want to create a YouTube channel.
quote.speaker: Mike

ideas.delivery: The operator flies a thermal drone over the relevant property, locates a heat signature, uses the zoom camera to identify it, and helps the hunter recover the animal. The transcript does not specify the full field workflow or how often the drone locates an animal.
unit_economics_claims: Mike said he made $50,000 during his first ten weeks of public deer recovery work in Ohio.
Mike stated a $550 fee if he found a deer and $450 if he did not.
Mike said a tracking dog cost about $350 and that customers paid a $200 premium for his service because it avoided disturbing other deer.
ideas.startup_cost: The guest bought a drone, but its price and other startup costs are not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Chris suggests break-even came within a couple of weeks (Mike does not state this explicitly); Mike says he made $50,000 in his first ten weeks of public deer recovery work.

acquisition.how: Videos, listings, and search traffic can bring inbound enquiries, but the guest's launch depended on expo attendance, printed materials, and word of mouth.

onboarding.how: A person needs to understand the hunter's situation, confirm location and permissions, and coordinate a time to search.

delivery.how: A pilot must physically attend the property and operate or supervise a drone search.

billing.how: A booking and payment flow could be automated, but no billing system is described and the fee depends on the search result.

support.how: Hunters need human coordination around an urgent, location-specific search and recovery.

uk_applicability.notes: Thermal search and deer recovery could be relevant in the UK, but hunting practices, wildlife rules, land access, and drone regulations differ from Ohio and other US states.

risks: Mike says legality was unclear when he began and that he relied initially on an informal conversation with an Ohio natural resources official.
The service must not be used to locate a deer so that someone can then shoot it; the guest says the rules were later clarified in Ohio.
Mike says some hunters may take marginal shots because they expect a drone to find the deer.
A wounded deer may still be alive and could move after being found.

quotes.speaker: Mike

quotes.speaker: Mike

ideas.name: Drone pilot locator directory
ideas.one_liner: List independent drone deer recovery pilots on a searchable website and charge them an annual subscription.
ideas.business_model: Annual listing subscription from independent pilots.
ideas.customer: Independent drone deer recovery pilots seeking enquiries and hunters looking for a nearby pilot.
ideas.problem: Hunters need to find a recovery pilot in their area, while independent pilots need visibility.
ideas.offer: A zip-code search on the Drone Deer Recovery website shows nearby listed pilots and lets visitors contact them.

pricing.notes: Mike calls the listing price super cheap. The host estimated six figures in annual memberships from the listing count; that is the host's back-of-the-envelope estimate.

acquisition_channels.details: Hunters search for drone deer recovery pilots and use the website's zip-code lookup.

quote.text: And people that search for deer recovery people in their area. If they're on the drone do recovery website, they put in their zip code.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: The guest's videos help drive attention and traffic to the directory.

quote.text: we're getting anywhere from 2.5 to 3 million views on YouTube, Tik Tok, Instagram. So maybe some of those weren't literally looking for a a pilot.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Mike says he drives traffic to listed pilots through the website and social content.

quote.text: It gives you a drop down of who's close by and then they just click on contact pilot and then it'll text them the phone number so we can track exactly how many people go to the website
quote.speaker: Mike

ideas.delivery: The site accepts pilot listings, takes a visitor's zip code, displays nearby operators, and provides a contact action that texts the pilot's phone number. Mike says the website tracks traffic and contact clicks.
unit_economics_claims: Mike charges $500 per year for a pilot listing.
Mike said there were about 200 to 300 pilots listed.
Chris estimated six figures in annual membership revenue; this was an inference, not a reported result.
tools: Website contact form or contact action

acquisition.how: Search traffic and existing video audiences can bring pilots and hunters to the site, though content and directory growth still need ongoing work.

onboarding.how: Pilot sign-up and listing details could be collected online; the transcript does not describe whether review or approval is manual.

delivery.how: The website's zip-code lookup, nearby pilot results, and contact action are software-delivered.

billing.how: An annual subscription is suited to recurring online billing, but no automatic renewal or payment workflow is stated.

support.how: Listing questions, disputes, and directory maintenance may require human help; no support system is described.

uk_applicability.notes: A searchable directory and subscription model work in the UK, but the number of operators, hunting market, and rules for drone use in wildlife recovery may differ.

risks: Mike says he did not trademark the three-word name early enough, after it had become generic language, and that similarly named businesses caused market confusion.
Directory value depends on traffic, accurate listings, and enough pilots in the areas where hunters search.
The host's six-figure revenue estimate is not a verified figure from Mike.

tactics.name: Launch a service with a simple live demonstration
steps: Buy or borrow a drone capable of producing useful thermal footage.
Film a simple demonstration on your own property, such as showing a thermal view and then identifying the subject with a zoom camera.
Display the footage at an event attended by likely customers.
Bring business cards and small takeaways; Mike says he ran out of both.

tactics.name: Use customer feedback to set an initial price
steps: Ask potential customers what they expect the service to cost.
Treat feedback carefully when respondents may not be the buyer, but use specific comparisons to understand the value they see.
Mike initially considered $250 to $350, heard that the service was worth more, and later set a higher price with a different fee if no deer was found.

warnings.warning: Do not rely only on informal legal advice for drone deer recovery. Mike says the rules were initially unclear, and he later met local game wardens and watched the regulations change.
Do not use a drone to locate a deer so that it can then be shot. Mike says the official he contacted supported recovery only, not using the drone to find and shoot the deer.
Chris's idea of flying a drone at a farmer's property without permission was challenged by Mike, who said he needed permission to fly over the land.
Mike says he waited too long to trademark Drone Deer Recovery; the phrase became generic and similarly named operators caused customer confusion.
Mike says he does not recommend farmers' chemicals because a poor result could lead them to blame both the product and the drone application.
The guest says heavy-lift spraying requires multiple licenses and FAA paperwork, and describes that process as difficult and slow.
Mike says some hunters may take marginal shots because they expect a drone to find the deer, creating an ethical concern.
The host's AI employee promotion for HighLevel and promotion of TKOowners.com are promotional segments, not evidence about the guest's drone business.

evidence_quality.rationale: Mike is a first-hand operator who describes customer acquisition, pricing, equipment, and licensing in detail. His large profit, revenue, margin, market-size, and growth claims are not independently verified, and some figures are delivered through an auto-caption transcript with apparent recognition errors.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Mike sells DJI drones, spray rigs and trailers, offers financing, a 137 Fastpass program and a how-to-start booklet promoted via Instagram ads, so his upbeat profit claims also act as sales marketing. Chris has a HighLevel sponsor read and promotes his TKOowners.com community.

extraction.review_notes: The extraction is thorough and generally accurate, with good coverage of pricing, acreage and licensing claims and appropriate hypothetical flags on host calculations. The main problems are treating the $132k as profit when Mike only said 'made', a quote that put Chris's six-figure estimate under Mike's name, a few misattributions and misspellings, and a missed booklet/paid-ads product. Mike's equipment-sales interest deserved more weight in the promotional-conflict field. UK applicability for drone crop spraying was overstated given the UK's restrictions on aerial pesticide application.
